``` ::: ::: ## 2.2 Unsupervised Discretization Discretization transforms a **continuous attribute** into a **categorical attribute**. In unsupervised discretization, boundaries are selected without class labels. We use Iris `petal length (cm)`. ::: {#ae9960b2 .cell execution_count=4} ``` {.python .cell-code} petal_length = iris[[ "petal length (cm)" ]] petal_length.describe() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=4} ```{=html}
petal length (cm)
count 150.000000
mean 3.758000
std 1.765298
min 1.000000
25% 1.600000
50% 4.350000
75% 5.100000
max 6.900000
``` ::: ::: `KBinsDiscretizer` divides a numerical attribute into bins according to the selected `strategy`. ### Equal Width Equal-width discretization divides the value range into intervals with the same width. ::: {#770b5159 .cell execution_count=5} ``` {.python .cell-code} uniform = KBinsDiscretizer( n_bins=3, encode="ordinal", strategy="uniform", subsample=None, ) uniform_bins = uniform.fit_transform( petal_length ) uniform.bin_edges_[0] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=5} ``` array([1. , 2.96666667, 4.93333333, 6.9 ]) ``` ::: ::: The transformed values are ordinal bin numbers. We map them to categorical labels to make the discretized representation easier to read. ::: {#bc0b3e60 .cell execution_count=6} ``` {.python .cell-code} label_mapping = { 0: "low", 1: "medium", 2: "high", } uniform_result = pd.DataFrame({ "petal_length": ( petal_length[ "petal length (cm)" ] ), "category": ( pd.Series( uniform_bins.ravel() ) .replace(label_mapping) ), }) uniform_result.head() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=6} ```{=html}
petal_length category
0 1.4 low
1 1.4 low
2 1.3 low
3 1.5 low
4 1.4 low
``` ::: ::: ### Equal Frequency Equal-frequency discretization tries to place a similar number of objects in each interval. ::: {.callout-important title="Q. Practice"} Implement `equal_frequency_discretize()` in `lab02_2.py`. Create an equal-frequency discretizer with three bins and transform `petal_length`. **Hint:** Use `strategy="quantile"` and `fit_transform()`. ::: {#1b17e8ac .cell execution_count=7} ``` {.python .cell-code} quantile, quantile_bins = equal_frequency_discretize( petal_length, n_bins=3, ) quantile.bin_edges_[0] ``` ::: ::: ### Clustering-Based K-means discretization places boundaries according to one-dimensional clusters. ::: {#fc6d41be .cell execution_count=8} ``` {.python .cell-code} kmeans = KBinsDiscretizer( n_bins=3, encode="ordinal", strategy="kmeans", subsample=None, ) kmeans_bins = kmeans.fit_transform( petal_length ) kmeans.bin_edges_[0] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=7} ``` array([1. , 2.87637037, 4.95950081, 6.9 ]) ``` ::: ::: Equal width considers the value range, while equal frequency considers the number of objects in each interval. Neither method necessarily finds natural groups in the data. Clustering-based discretization uses the data distribution to place boundaries. ::: {#bf5f0757 .cell execution_count=9} ``` {.python .cell-code} boundaries = { "Equal width": uniform.bin_edges_[0], "Equal frequency": quantile.bin_edges_[0], "K-means": kmeans.bin_edges_[0], } plot_discretization( petal_length, boundaries, title="Three Discretization Strategies", ) ``` ::: ::: {.callout-tip title="Think"} Why can the same attribute have different boundaries under the three strategies? Equal width splits the value range, equal frequency splits by count, and k-means follows clusters. Each method optimizes a different criterion. ::: ## 2.3 Supervised Discretization With class labels, we can evaluate whether a boundary creates intervals that mostly contain objects from the same class. A good interval has low class mixing. The entropy of interval $i$ is $$ e_i = -\sum_{j=1}^{k} p_{ij} \log_2 p_{ij}, $$ where $p_{ij}$ is the fraction of objects in interval $i$ that belong to class $j$. `entropy()` is provided in `helper.py`. A pure interval has entropy 0, while an evenly mixed interval has higher entropy. ::: {#406e998a .cell execution_count=10} ``` {.python .cell-code} pure = np.array([ "A", "A", "A", "A", ]) mixed = np.array([ "A", "A", "B", "B", ]) print( "Pure entropy:", entropy(pure), ) print( "Mixed entropy:", entropy(mixed), ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Pure entropy: -0.0 Mixed entropy: 1.0 ``` ::: ::: To evaluate a candidate boundary, we first choose one threshold and split the attribute into two intervals. Here, `threshold = 2.45` is one candidate boundary for `petal length (cm)`. ::: {#fe4c623d .cell execution_count=11} ``` {.python .cell-code} x = iris[ "petal length (cm)" ].to_numpy() y = iris[ "species" ].to_numpy() threshold = 2.45 left_labels = y[ x <= threshold ] right_labels = y[ x > threshold ] left_entropy = entropy( left_labels ) right_entropy = entropy( right_labels ) print( "Left entropy:", round(left_entropy, 4), ) print( "Right entropy:", round(right_entropy, 4), ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Left entropy: -0.0 Right entropy: 1.0 ``` ::: ::: The total quality of the split is the weighted average of interval entropies: $$ e = \sum_{i=1}^{n} w_i e_i, \qquad w_i = \frac{m_i}{m}. $$ For two intervals, this becomes $$ e = \frac{n_L}{n}e_L + \frac{n_R}{n}e_R. $$ ::: {.callout-important title="Q. Practice"} Implement `weighted_split_entropy()` in `lab02_2.py`. It should return the weighted entropy of the two intervals. **Hint:** Weight each interval entropy by the proportion of objects in that interval. Use `entropy()` from `helper.py`. ::: {#6355683a .cell execution_count=12} ``` {.python .cell-code} split_score = weighted_split_entropy( left_labels, right_labels, ) print( "Weighted entropy:", round(split_score, 4), ) ``` ::: ::: A good supervised boundary minimizes the weighted entropy. We can repeat the same calculation for all candidate thresholds. ::: {#15163d07 .cell execution_count=13} ``` {.python .cell-code} def split_entropy( x, y, threshold, ): left = y[ x <= threshold ] right = y[ x > threshold ] if ( len(left) == 0 or len(right) == 0 ): return np.inf return ( len(left) / len(y) * entropy(left) + len(right) / len(y) * entropy(right) ) unique_values = np.sort( np.unique(x) ) candidate_thresholds = ( unique_values[:-1] + unique_values[1:] ) / 2 scores = np.array([ split_entropy( x, y, threshold, ) for threshold in candidate_thresholds ]) best_index = np.argmin( scores ) best_threshold = ( candidate_thresholds[ best_index ] ) print( "Best threshold:", best_threshold, ) print( "Minimum weighted entropy:", round( scores[best_index], 4, ), ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Best threshold: 2.45 Minimum weighted entropy: 0.6667 ``` ::: ::: ::: {#a0e597a6 .cell execution_count=14} ``` {.python .cell-code} plot_entropy_thresholds( candidate_thresholds, scores, best_threshold, ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![Weighted entropy for candidate thresholds](Lab02-2_files/figure-html/cell-15-output-1.png){} ::: ::: ::: {.callout-tip title="Think"} What information is used here that was not used in unsupervised discretization? Class labels. Unsupervised methods look only at the attribute values. ::: ## 2.4 Binarization Binarization transforms a categorical attribute into one or more **binary attributes**. For a categorical attribute with $m$ categories, there are two common representations: - **Compact encoding:** assign integers from $0$ to $m-1$ and represent them using $\lceil \log_2 m \rceil$ binary variables. - **One-hot encoding:** create one binary variable for each category. For example, five categories require only three binary variables with compact encoding, but five variables with one-hot encoding. Compact encoding uses fewer variables, but its binary codes can create associations that are not present in the original categorical data. In this lab, we use **one-hot encoding** with `pd.get_dummies()`. ::: {#abf24a01 .cell execution_count=15} ``` {.python .cell-code} embarked_binary = pd.get_dummies( titanic["embarked"], prefix="embarked", dtype=int, ) embarked_binary.head() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=12} ```{=html}
embarked_C embarked_Q embarked_S
0 0 0 1
1 1 0 0
2 0 0 1
3 0 0 1
4 0 0 1
``` ::: ::: Each binary column represents one category. A value of `1` indicates that the passenger belongs to that category, and `0` indicates otherwise. ::: {#5c12b852 .cell execution_count=16} ``` {.python .cell-code} num_categories = ( titanic["embarked"] .nunique() ) compact_variables = int( np.ceil( np.log2( num_categories ) ) ) print( "Number of categories:", num_categories, ) print( "Compact variables:", compact_variables, ) print( "One-hot variables:", embarked_binary.shape[1], ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Number of categories: 3 Compact variables: 2 One-hot variables: 3 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.callout-important title="Q. Practice"} Implement `binarize_categorical()` in `lab02_2.py`. Convert the categorical attribute `sex` into binary variables. **Hint:** Use `pd.get_dummies()` with `prefix="sex"` and `dtype=int`. ::: {#eccfdd31 .cell execution_count=17} ``` {.python .cell-code} sex_binary = binarize_categorical( titanic["sex"], prefix="sex", ) sex_binary.head() ``` ::: ::: ::: {.callout-tip title="Think"} If a categorical attribute has five categories, how many binary variables are required by compact encoding and one-hot encoding? Compact encoding needs $\lceil \log_2 5 \rceil = 3$ binary variables. One-hot encoding needs 5. ::: ::: {.callout-tip title="Think"} Why can compact encoding introduce relationships that were not present in the original categorical attribute? The bit patterns impose closeness that the original categories do not have. Two categories can look similar only because they share bits. ::: ## 2.5 Functional Transformation A functional transformation applies a mathematical function to a numerical attribute. Titanic `fare` has a long right tail, so we apply a log transformation. ::: {#5c22b700 .cell execution_count=18} ``` {.python .cell-code} fare = ( titanic["fare"] .dropna() ) fare_log = np.log1p( fare ) pd.DataFrame({ "fare": fare.head(), "log_fare": fare_log.head(), }) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=14} ```{=html}
fare log_fare
0 7.2500 2.110213
1 71.2833 4.280593
2 7.9250 2.188856
3 53.1000 3.990834
4 8.0500 2.202765
``` ::: ::: ::: {#04731885 .cell execution_count=19} ``` {.python .cell-code} plot_log_transformation( fare, fare_log, ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![Fare before and after log transformation](Lab02-2_files/figure-html/cell-20-output-1.png){} ::: ::: ::: {.callout-tip title="Think"} What happened to the long right tail after the log transformation? The tail is compressed. Large fares move closer to the rest of the distribution. ::: ## 2.6 Scaling Scaling places numerical attributes on comparable scales. We compare Titanic `age` and `fare`. ::: {#a1b76bc1 .cell execution_count=20} ``` {.python .cell-code} X = titanic[[ "age", "fare", ]].copy() X["age"] = ( X["age"] .fillna( X["age"].median() ) ) X["fare"] = ( X["fare"] .fillna( X["fare"].median() ) ) X.describe() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=16} ```{=html}
age fare

25% 22.000000 7.910400

``` ::: ::: For Z-score standardization, $$ z = \frac{x-\mu}{\sigma}. $$ ::: {#f7cc7b09 .cell execution_count=21} ``` {.python .cell-code} zscore = ( X - X.mean() ) / X.std( ddof=0 ) zscore.describe().round(3) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=17} ```{=html}

Practice"} Implement `minmax_scale()` and `robust_scale()` in `lab02_2.py`. $$ x_{\text{min-max}} = \frac{x-x_{\min}} {x_{\max}-x_{\min}} $$ $$ x_{\text{robust}} = \frac{x-\text{median}(x)} {IQR(x)} $$ **Hint:** For the IQR, use `X.quantile(0.75) - X.quantile(0.25)`. ::: {#5c22a93c .cell execution_count=23} ``` {.python .cell-code} minmax = minmax_scale(X) robust = robust_scale(X) print( "Min-Max" ) display( minmax.describe().round(3) ) print( "Robust" ) display( robust.describe().round(3) ) ``` ::: ::: ::: {#39918ab1 .cell execution_count=24} ``` {.python .cell-code} plot_scaling({ "Original": X, "Min-Max": minmax, "Mean normalization": mean_normalized, "Z-score": zscore, "Robust": robust, }) ``` ::: ::: {.callout-tip title="Think"} Which scaling method uses the median and IQR instead of the mean and standard deviation? Robust scaling. :::
